body:
> First Pipe in @edge/runtime dose not process possible reader error, which should have destroyed res with that error

The `pipeBodyStreamToResponse` is designed so that the caller handles closing the response (in case it wants to send more data). We just need a `.then(destroy, destroy)` to handle.

> Meanwhile it checks open state in every chunk cycle which is not as fast as you think.

`open` is a local variable, so I'm not sure what you mean.

> Third it is another package, and do we really need to import another or just leave this method alone?

This is a Vercel library consuming another Vercel library, and I think commonly used inside Next.js (which will have already loaded the `edge-runtime` library). In that case, changing will actually reduce code at runtime. And if this isn't being used by a Next.js server, a bundler will be able to strip out everything not used by us.

body:
This action is a great example of the power of the Lusat action builder.

It's very similar to defining procedures in the beloved [**tRPC**](https://trpc.io), in fact it uses a similar builder syntax, input schema system, and type inference.

By calling `action()` we start a new builder chain. 

We can add a description, compatible with OpenAI Function Calling through the `gptFunctions` adapter, with the `.describe()` builder method. This is the same as the syntax for describing individual parts of the input schema through Zod's own `.describe()` methods.

Then, we define our input schema with Zod and the `.input()` builder method. This will not only register a Zod schema with which Lusat will automatically parse & validate input data when the action is called autonomously by the AI, but also provides the inferred typesafety we need to define our handler without manually writing types. Two birds, one stone.

Finally, the `.handle()` method ends the builder chain, and guarantees that our action handler consumes the type parsed by the input schema, completing our action.

Same process more or less applies to the other functions converted 1-to-1 from @Zakinator123 and @jaredpalmer's manual example.

body:
This code is designed to make the useChat hook reactive so that any changes in the API state are automatically reflected in the `useChat` hook. In SolidJS, state primitives (signals) are functions that need to be called to retrieve the latest value of the API state. In contrast, React allows you to directly read the API state to get its latest value. This fundamental difference necessitated my changes.

```js
const [api, setApi] = createSignal();
const chat = useChat({ api }); // Here, api is a function, hence it will be reactive.
```

The current `StreamingParser` does not expose its internal state, this `root` is the mutable partially parsed object.

body:
```suggestion
One way to understand this concept is through a Lego analogy. Imagine a 10,000 piece Lego model that, once built, cannot be easily transported because it is fragile. By taking the model apart, it can be easily transported, and then rebuilt following the steps outlined in the instructions pamphlet. In this way, the instructions pamphlet is a proxy to the physical structure. Similarly, AI State provides a serialisable (JSON) representation of your UI that can be passed back and forth to the model.
```

body:
An install or build command (well, all of the `scripts` commands, I believe) with a Node version that isn't `18.x.x` or `20.x.x` will output a warning as below at the start of command execution.

I think this is desirable, and preferred to (say) hard-failing, though we could do that too to force a maintainer to have a known good version (see the PR description for more).

There should be no effect for those with a compatible Node version.

It is possible it could be spammy or annoying for devs that consciously choose to use a version they know isn't officially supported. We could remove the engine spec and just rely on the small update to the contributing docs as an FYI.

Note that I believe non-maintainers installing the AI SDK with a Node engine that doesn't fit the spec will also see the warning. Again, this seems ok to me. We don't block/disallow the install, but we let them know their mileage may vary.

```
 WARN  Unsupported engine: wanted: {"node":"^18.0.0 || ^20.0.0"} (current: {"node":"v23.0.0","pnpm":"9.12.2"})
```

Without this we get a `vitest - cjs format deprecation` warning. We have other areas in the codebase similarly, but since this is a new package I thought to try shifting to 'module'.

The main thought is that in older versions of Node esm was , but we're new enough that this should be fine:
> ESM support was experimental before Node.js 12.0.0 and became stable in Node.js 12.22.0, 14.17.0, and 16.0.0+.

Other notes:
- clients using this would need to `import` rather than `require` (but the intent of this package/module is just to run codemods, so it's executing a binary which will work with ESM if Node does)
- there can be build tool/bundler support issues, but again this package isn't intended to be pulled in and used by others
- it's possible to dual-package as CJS and ESM, or transpile back to CJS I believe

I recognize the value of staying consistent. The default is CJS, and we don't specify in any of our other `packages` (though two examples do use '"module"').

Open to your thought, it's be nice to remove deprecation bits when we can and it feels like we're at the cusp of being able to move to ESM community/tool wise. Trying it here could be a useful staging, though not a perfect test since it's not intended for use by others directly as the other packages are.

body:
This PR is a good example of one where ideally we'd have fuller refactoring, multifile, static-analysis-based infra to do it right.

The PR aims to address all three of the Provider "Removed `topK` setting" cases [here](https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/troubleshooting/migration-guide/migration-guide-4-0#removed-topk-setting) and below.

I think landing this PR as is should be fine. To explain what I have in mind for any feedback/future thoughts:
- I definitely think this codemod should remove `topK` from provider create methods
- Ideally we would then (as we do in a limited set of cases here) proactively *add* topK with the value it had in the previously removed line(s)
- However, it could well be the case that the involved API calls using the model in question are all outside of this file. Or, that they use an intermediate variable to hold the model, etc.
  - the LLM has proposed updates to the codemod (not in this PR) to perform at least limited static analysis re: variable assigns that could partially address the above
  - this is also an area where a jscodeshift util lib of routines could help us as others have surely done work here already
- So, perhaps we get ourselves in trouble by trying to do such a fix and taking it only partway. Calls we miss will "silently fail" in that they will just lose the `topK` value they used to have.
- An alternative (or in-addition, which would be easy to add) would be to drop a comment where we remove `topK` from a provider construction and remind the dev to review any generate/stream API calls using models created from the instance to potentially add `topK` back in (or otherwise effect via their own wrapper logic, etc.).

Model ID case mismatch\: The type definition specifies `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-V1'` \(uppercase V\) but the runtime validation check uses `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-v1'` \(lowercase v\)\, causing the 1024 document limit validation to never trigger when using the typed model ID\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## Type definition case mismatch prevents 1024 document limit validation

**What fails\:** `TogetherAIRerankingModelId` type defines model as `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-V1'` \(uppercase V\) but runtime check in `TogetherAIRerankingModel.doRerank()` uses `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-v1'` \(lowercase v\)\, causing string comparison to fail

**How to reproduce\:**

```typescript
const model = togetherai.rerankingModel('Salesforce/Llama-Rank-V1'); // Type-suggested ID
const docs = Array.from({ length: 1025 }, (_, i) => `doc  
```

**Result\:** No `TooManyDocumentsForRerankingError` thrown at line 77 check because `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-V1' === 'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-v1'` evaluates to `false`

**Expected\:** Error should throw when exceeding 1024 documents per [TogetherAI API docs](https://docs.together.ai/reference/rerank-1) which uses `Salesforce/Llama-Rank-v1` \(lowercase v\)

**Fix\:** Changed type definition to `'Salesforce/Llama-Rank-v1'` to match official API model ID format and runtime validation check

</details>

The TooManyDocumentsForRerankingError constructor expects `documentsCount: number`\, but callers pass `documents: Array` or use inconsistent property names\, causing incorrect error objects\.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.ts b/packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.ts index e89ab6d7c..e60a45c01 100644 --- a/packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.ts +++ b/packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.ts @@ -100,7 +100,7 @@ Only applicable for HTTP-based providers. provider: model.provider, modelId: model.modelId, maxDocumentsPerCall, - documents: values, + documentsCount: values.length, }); } const { maxRetries, retry } = prepareRetries({ diff --git a/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-reranking-model.ts b/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-reranking-model.ts index 14b329b47..10a7887df 100644 --- a/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-reranking-model.ts +++ b/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-reranking-model.ts @@ -58,7 +58,7 @@ export class BedrockRerankingModel provider: this.provider, modelId: this.modelId, maxDocumentsPerCall: this.maxDocumentsPerCall, - documents: values, + documentsCount: values.length, }); } // only cohere model supports json documents (values) diff --git a/packages/togetherai/src/togetherai-reranking-model.ts b/packages/togetherai/src/togetherai-reranking-model.ts index 75e2831de..d30723cf0 100644 --- a/packages/togetherai/src/togetherai-reranking-model.ts +++ b/packages/togetherai/src/togetherai-reranking-model.ts @@ -69,7 +69,7 @@ export class TogetherAIRerankingModel provider: this.provider, modelId: this.modelId, maxDocumentsPerCall: this.maxDocumentsPerCall, - documents: values, + documentsCount: values.length, }); } @@ -79,7 +79,7 @@ export class TogetherAIRerankingModel provider: this.provider, modelId: this.modelId, maxDocumentsPerCall: 1024, - documents: values, + documentsCount: values.length, }); } ```
### Analysis ## TooManyDocumentsForRerankingError receives incorrect property name causing undefined documentsCount **What fails\:** The `TooManyDocumentsForRerankingError` constructor expects `documentsCount: number`\, but callers in 3 packages pass `documents: Array` instead of `documentsCount: number`\, resulting in the `documentsCount` property being `undefined` when the error is thrown\. **How to reproduce\:** ```typescript // packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.ts (line 103) throw new TooManyDocumentsForRerankingError({ provider: model.provider, modelId: model.modelId, maxDocumentsPerCall, documents: values, // WRONG: passes array instead of count }); ``` **Result\:** TypeScript compile error TS2353\: ``` error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'documents' does not exist in type '{ provider: string; modelId: string; maxDocumentsPerCall: number; documentsCount: number; }'. ``` At runtime\, the error object would have `documentsCount: undefined`\, causing error messages to display \"undefined documents were provided\" instead of the actual count\. **Expected behavior\:** Per the error class constructor definition \(packages\/provider\/src\/errors\/too\-many\-documents\-for\-reranking\-error\.ts\)\, callers should pass `documentsCount: values.length` instead of `documents: values`\. **Affected files\:** * packages\/ai\/src\/rerank\/rerank\.ts \(line 103\)\: Fixed * packages\/amazon\-bedrock\/src\/bedrock\-reranking\-model\.ts \(line 61\)\: Fixed * packages\/togetherai\/src\/togetherai\-reranking\-model\.ts \(lines 72\, 82\)\: Fixed \- two occurrences * packages\/cohere\/src\/reranking\/cohere\-reranking\-model\.ts \(line 68\)\: Already correct **Tests\:** All related tests pass after fixes\: * `packages/ai/src/rerank/rerank.test.ts`\: 11 tests passed * `packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-reranking-model.test.ts`\: 5 tests passed

```suggestion
}
```

<details>

<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## TogetherAI example uses wrong provider key in reranking options

**What fails\:** The example at `examples/ai-core/src/rerank/togetherai-object.ts` specifies provider options under the key `cohere:` instead of `togetherai:`\, causing the options \(specifically `rankFields`\) to be ignored by the TogetherAI reranking model\.

**How to reproduce\:**

1.  Look at `packages/togetherai/src/reranking/togetherai-reranking-model.ts` line 56 \- it calls `parseProviderOptions({ provider: 'togetherai', ... })`
2.  The `parseProviderOptions` function at `packages/provider-utils/src/parse-provider-options.ts` line 10 looks for `providerOptions[provider]` \- in this case `providerOptions['togetherai']`
3.  The example uses `providerOptions: { cohere: { rankFields: [...] } }`\, so it\'s looking for the wrong key
4.  Result\: `parseProviderOptions` returns `undefined` because `providerOptions['togetherai']` doesn\'t exist\, and `rankFields` is never sent to the API

**Expected behavior\:** The example should use `togetherai:` as the provider key\, matching the actual provider identifier passed to `parseProviderOptions`\. This matches the pattern used in the test suite at `packages/togetherai/src/reranking/togetherai-reranking-model.test.ts` lines 40 and 68\, and aligns with how the Cohere example correctly uses `cohere:` for the Cohere provider\.

**Why this is a bug\:** The `parseProviderOptions` function uses the provider name as a key to look up options in the `providerOptions` object\. Using the wrong provider key causes the options to not be found and results in a silent failure where the options are ignored\.

</details>

- create and use a different type here that only has what we do want to expose to the concrete impl (`defaultObjectGenerationMode`)
- put the bits we want to expose in settings instead, and maybe merge that into the config in `chatModel` impl logic
- make the config params optional instead of required and add validation logic elsewhere if needed
- add a method in `OpenAICompatibleProvider` or exported as part of this file that allows the concrete impls to construct a config, with args being only the bits we need from the concrete impl (but then we may want to change how the Provider is instantiated since currently we do it as part of that flow, and then the Provider pattern is more deviant from our others, which wouldn't be the end of the world but is nice to avoid)

body:
The only difference I see is for the older PaLM models. Here is my understanding:

[GenAI Harm Categories](https://ai.google.dev/api/generate-content#harmblockthreshold)
[Vertex Harm Categories](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/aiplatform/latest/google.cloud.aiplatform_v1.types.HarmCategory)

The PaLM entries in the GenAI link are missing:

```
HARM_CATEGORY_DEROGATORY | PaLM - Negative or harmful comments targeting identity and/or protected attribute.
HARM_CATEGORY_TOXICITY | PaLM - Content that is rude, disrespectful, or profane.
HARM_CATEGORY_VIOLENCE | PaLM - Describes scenarios depicting violence against an individual or group, or general descriptions of gore.
HARM_CATEGORY_SEXUAL | PaLM - Contains references to sexual acts or other lewd content.
HARM_CATEGORY_MEDICAL | PaLM - Promotes unchecked medical advice.
HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS | PaLM - Dangerous content that promotes, facilitates, or encourages harmful acts.
```

I assume these have been updated over time. Based on the current specs linked above, my take is that this PR is newly updated to reflect the latest, and the only consideration is whether to add the PaLM entries:
- we were missing the `HARM_CATEGORY_UNSPECIFIED` in GenAI but they are relevant there
- we were missing `HARM_CATEGORY_CIVIC_INTEGRITY` in both GenAI and Vertex, and it's relevant in both
- we were missing the PaLM entries above in both. GenAI spec has the PaLM entries and Vertex doesn't
- https://ai.google.dev/palm_docs notes "Warning: The PaLM API is decomissioned. The Vertex AI PaLM API [is scheduled to be decomissioned in October 2024](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/model-reference/text). Please upgrade to the Gemini API. Learn more about this in the [PaLM API deprecation guide](https://ai.google.dev/palm_docs/deprecation)."

It is not clear to me that the PaLM models are a forward-going concern, so I would personally omit them for now.

FYI (and related to the cached Auth instance above in a way), in final testing (pack/deploy iterating) I noted the `node` route of `next-google-vertex` of course doesn't work as I haven't made a creds file available. I started looking into making one available to my deployment just to test fully, or learn more as to how folks commonly deploy this in Node, and found this:

https://googleapis.dev/nodejs/google-auth-library/9.14.1/

Under the **Loading credentials from environment variables** section:

> Instead of loading credentials from a key file, you can also provide them using an environment variable and the GoogleAuth.fromJSON() method. This is particularly convenient for systems that deploy directly from source control (Heroku, App Engine, etc).

I don't think adding optional support for this needs to block shipping, since:
- folks can effectively implement this themselves differently via the `googleAuthOptions` setting params, or with a custom headers hook
- it doesn't appear there's a standard env var they use to trigger this
- I have had in mind that most folks ship a creds file if they're deploying this way (or use one of the other methods). One of the methods in fact tries to just "do the right thing", see **Choosing the correct credential type automatically**. I briefly tested this but it required enabling another GCP API (DNS related) and I haven't revisited yet.
- we can wait to hear if there are requests and respond quickly with this or whatever else is requested

Checkpointing my understanding and design choice for potential discussion:
- `timestamp` - intended to be, if provider produces such, the timestamp associated with the inference request. Fallbacks could be (1) our own intra-image-model-impl pre-post-to-api timestamp, or (2) an intra-generate-image timestamp. I've gone with (2) for all cases here to reduce the amount of code we need in image models, and as I'm not aware of the providers producing what we want. It would at least be more accurate to track timestamp in each model just before we post, and ship that back in `result.response.timestamp`. Is it worth the extra complexity?
- `modelId`: for language models we have them populate and return this, however here we know what it is, so it felt redundant and again saved on model-impl-side complexity to just use what we had here.

body:
I have that here because let's say you pass a tool to the aisdk with an `execute()` method. That means you'll get two responses from the provider. 

- The first response will have the `currentReasoningDetails`, but that isn't extracted out to the final `generateText` response from the provider, because:
- the SECOND run (after the tool result is done), will overwrite the reasoning details. 

This code just appends the reasoning details every time this is called for that interaction, ensuring we always get the reasoning populated in the final response, regardless of provider.

In the event this logic is removed, on `generateText` calls with tool invocations, we experience the issue described in https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/4980#issuecomment-2691631997

body:
My hesitation here is that if I do:

```typescript
const BedrockReasoningConfigOptionsSchema = z
  .object({
    type: z.union([z.literal('enabled'), z.literal('disabled')]),
  })
  .and(
    z.union([
      z.object({ budget_tokens: z.number() }),
      z.object({ budgetTokens: z.number() }),
    ])
  )
  .nullish();
```

Instead of the transform, it will break type checking here:

```typescript
const thinkingBudget = reasoningConfigOptions.data?.budget_tokens ??
      reasoningConfigOptions.data?.budgetTokens;
```

I can fix that using `in`, but doesn't seem as clean?

e.g.

```typescript
const thinkingBudget = reasoningConfigOptions.data && 
      ('budget_tokens' in reasoningConfigOptions.data 
        ? reasoningConfigOptions.data.budget_tokens 
        : 'budgetTokens' in reasoningConfigOptions.data 
          ? reasoningConfigOptions.data.budgetTokens 
          : undefined);
```

I pushed that in: [35cf123](https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/5088/commits/35cf1234a64586c135015708302cb4207743ef6e)

This PR introduces the foundations for transcribing audio by adding a new experimental_generateTranscript function along with the necessary implementation, tests, documentation, and integration in the AI SDK.  
- Added comprehensive audio input conversion utilities.  
- Implemented and integrated the generateTranscript function with the transcription provider.  
- Enhanced test coverage and documentation for the new transcription capabilities.

author: lgrammel

body:
I see your point! I had opted for this since we offer provider options at the message level _and_ function level (also will respond and let the user know they should pass to generateText)

But I'm not sure if it's worth introducing a breaking change by throwing / preventing a mixed array of messages, e.g. in situations where users are dynamically appending messages, because the `messages` parameter does technically accept all kinds. I wonder how many users are actually doing this!

Not a strongly held opinion, happy to enforce uniform messages array if you feel strongly!
author: iteratetograceness

body:
> I had opted for this since we offer provider options at the message level and function level (also will respond and let the user know they should pass to generateText)

Interesting - my sense is that there is a larger problem here, we need to provider the user with a standardized way of adding provider options that are part-specific (e.g. openai image detail) when they have ui messages. Currently they would need to run `convertToCoreMessages` and then map the core messages, but I don't think we have this documented.

My concern is that we enable the user to have a myriad of patterns if we support mixed messages, and then later we have to support that (also in persistence patterns).

2 alternatives I can think of:
- supporting `providerOptions` on UI messages and parts (somewhat reluctant to do this)
- documenting a pattern of how to add image part details (even if it's clunky)

Not saying that we should not support mixed arrays as you suggested, just want to have a better understanding what it would mean for the users and also for our own maintenance / compatibility in the future. Good point on the backwards compat.

body:
If the stream has ended, we send the assistant message generated as a SSE to the client to resolve. The goal here is to make that event only available for 15 seconds instead of it being persistent forever. For the non-race condition case, the endpoint will return empty after the stream has ended. For the race-condition case, the endpoint returns the SSE so figured it would be good to return empty after 15 seconds for consistency.

It is worth noting that there is no drawback if we remove this check – do you think we should keep it or not?

I can comment the reasoning if we do decide to keep it.

body: @lgrammel, I tried a variation of https://colab.research.google.com/github/google-gemini/cookbook/blob/main/quickstarts/Get_started_thinking.ipynb with a valid API key, and it turns out the GEMINI api doesn't yet OFFICIALLY support (read: documented) `includeThoughts`. Looking at the proto definitions for the python client, `include_thoughts` isn't yet supported: (documented) https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/aiplatform/latest/google.cloud.aiplatform_v1.types.GenerationConfig.ThinkingConfig Compare this to the vertex api documentation, where `includeThoughts` IS supported: https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1/GenerationConfig#ThinkingConfig However, trying this in the notebook, we can see when we set a `thinkingBudget` and `includeThoughts`, the request IS valid, but it doesn't return thought candidates, despite using thinking tokens: --- So I suppose, in the Google Generative API, it WON'T provide the thoughts, but the request will still work likely it will eventually be supported. We should probably just remove the [15-google-generative-ai.mdx](https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/6261/files/c1264af0b981b44dc2254b9e6674c2dc39566b97#diff-9708c5f7984a6b6aa554bcb69e7fafb96b5b4dc80d91db3f1d18fab1cbebacda) file edits for now? --- Here's more photos playing around with the `ThinkingConfig`: --- TL;DR: While the parameter `include_thoughts` works on the Google Generative AI platform, it doesn't currently return the thought tokens from the response. It does work as expected in Vertex AI. Likely way forward is to remove the edits to [15-google-generative-ai.mdx](https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/6261/files/c1264af0b981b44dc2254b9e6674c2dc39566b97#diff-9708c5f7984a6b6aa554bcb69e7fafb96b5b4dc80d91db3f1d18fab1cbebacda) from this PR. body:
This will keep the raw base64 data, e.g. 
`IGcfqljA=`

And NOT `data:image/png;base64,IGcfqljA=`

I am open to suggestions on this, but I decided not to add the data URL scheme (RFC 2397), because:
- `mimeType` is optional on the `ImagePart`, and not always known
- current Uint8Array is raw data as well and is not aware of mimeTypes
- Telemetry backends can use the `mimeType` field, and there is lots of other heuristics to infer that this is base64

> wonder how far we should to here. usually we do this but it is also overhead 

I agree. I think we should do it for properties that we see repeatedly across providers and models. But e.g. not go overboard with things like `debug_latents` which is specific to a single model from `fal`

I also wonder if we should pass through provider options that we don't handle ourselves. Otherwise we will always play catch up whenever some model from some provider exposes a new information. We could do it in a way that clearly communicates that we don't take responsibility, like `.providerMetaData.fal.unsafe_otherData`  or similar.

body:
We need to be able to pass `reasoning.encrypted_content`: Includes an encrypted version of reasoning tokens in reasoning item outputs. This enables reasoning items to be used in multi-turn conversations when using the Responses API statelessly (like when the store parameter is set to false, or when an organization is enrolled in the zero data retention program).
It has also been added to, where I enforce the currently support types that we have also have implementation for in the framework.
```typescript
const openaiResponsesProviderOptionsSchema = z.object({
  metadata: z.any().nullish(),
  parallelToolCalls: z.boolean().nullish(),
  previousResponseId: z.string().nullish(),
  store: z.boolean().nullish(),
  user: z.string().nullish(),
  reasoningEffort: z.string().nullish(),
  strictJsonSchema: z.boolean().nullish(),
  instructions: z.string().nullish(),
  reasoningSummary: z.string().nullish(),
  serviceTier: z.enum(['auto', 'flex']).nullish(),
  include: z.array(z.enum(['reasoning.encrypted_content'])).nullish(),
});
```

I always use const since it plays well with discriminated unions, type hinting etc. I would say it is recommended to always do that when emitting something that is a literal and not a string.

```
// Without 'as const' - type is inferred as string
const event1 = { type: 'reasoning-start' }; // type: string

const event2 = { type: 'reasoning-start' as const }; // type: 'reasoning-start'
```

body:
The documentation shows conflicting import patterns for the Vivgrid provider, which will confuse developers about the correct API usage.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/content/providers/03-community-providers/06-vivgrid.mdx b/content/providers/03-community-providers/06-vivgrid.mdx index bae31710e..8909e9ffb 100644 --- a/content/providers/03-community-providers/06-vivgrid.mdx +++ b/content/providers/03-community-providers/06-vivgrid.mdx @@ -66,6 +66,12 @@ Obtain your API key from the [Vivgrid Console](https://console.vivgrid.com). You can import the default provider instance `vivgrid` from `@vivgrid/ai-sdk-provider`: +```typescript +import { vivgrid } from '@vivgrid/ai-sdk-provider'; +``` + +If you need a customized setup, you can import `createVivgrid` from `@vivgrid/ai-sdk-provider` and create a provider instance with your settings: + ```typescript import { createVivgrid } from '@vivgrid/ai-sdk-provider'; ```
### Analysis There's an inconsistency in how the Vivgrid provider is imported and used throughout the documentation: 1. **Lines 67-74** show the pattern: `import { createVivgrid }` followed by `const vivgrid = createVivgrid({ apiKey: ... })` 2. **Lines 102, 116, and 154** show the pattern: `import { vivgrid }` directly from the package This creates confusion about whether `vivgrid` is a factory function that needs to be created with `createVivgrid()`, or a direct import. The documentation should be consistent throughout - either show the factory pattern everywhere, or show the direct import pattern everywhere. This inconsistency will lead to developer confusion and potential runtime errors if they mix the patterns incorrectly.

The `streamObject` function is incorrectly being awaited\. The function returns a result object synchronously\, not a promise\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## Incorrect `await` usage with `streamObject` in Aihubmix documentation

**What fails\:** The `streamObject` example in `content/providers/03-community-providers/15-aihubmix.mdx` line 192 incorrectly uses `await` with `streamObject()`\, which returns a result object synchronously\, not a Promise\.

**How to reproduce\:** Copy the \"Stream Object\" example from the Aihubmix documentation and run it in a Node\.js\/TypeScript environment with AI SDK v4\.0\+\. The code would work but is using an outdated pattern from AI SDK 3\.4\.

**Result\:** The code shows `const result = await streamObject({...})` with the `await` keyword\, which is the old AI SDK 3\.4 pattern\.

**Expected\:** Per [AI SDK 4\.0 migration guide](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/migration-guides/migration-guide-4-0#streamobject-returns-immediately)\, `streamObject` returns immediately without needing `await`\. The correct pattern is `const result = streamObject({...})` \(without `await`\)\, which matches all other examples in the codebase including the \"Stream Text\" example on line 138 of the same file and the [official streamObject reference](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-object)\.

</details>

The `result.usage` and `result.object` properties are promises that must be awaited\, but the code accesses them without `await`\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## Missing `await` for Promise properties in streamObject example

**What fails\:** In `content/providers/03-community-providers/15-aihubmix.mdx` lines 213\-214\, the streamObject example accesses `result.usage` and `result.object` without `await`\, causing Promise objects to be logged instead of actual values\.

**How to reproduce\:**

```typescript
const result = await streamObject({ /* config */ });
for await (const objectPart of result.partialObjectStream) {}
console.log('Token usage:', result.usage);  // Logs: Promise { <pending> }
console.log('Final object:', result.object);  // Logs: Promise { <pending> }
```

**Result\:** Console logs display `Promise { <pending> }` instead of the actual token usage and final object values\, providing incorrect documentation to users\.

**Expected\:** Both properties should be awaited to display actual values\, consistent with\:

*   The streamText example \(lines 152\-153\) which correctly uses `await result.usage` and `await result.finishReason`
*   [AI SDK streamObject documentation](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-object) which specifies `usage: Promise<LanguageModelUsage>` and `object: Promise<T>`

</details>

body:
## Pull Request Overview

This PR adds support for detecting audio/webm media type to the `detect-media-type` utility. The change enables proper handling of WebM audio files generated by Chrome's MediaRecorder API, which was previously incorrectly identified as audio/wav and causing errors with the OpenAI transcription API.

- Adds WebM signature detection with magic bytes `[0x1a, 0x45, 0xdf, 0xa3]` and base64 prefix `GkXf`
- Includes comprehensive test coverage for both byte array and base64 string detection

### Reviewed Changes

Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated no comments.

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| packages/ai/src/util/detect-media-type.ts | Adds WebM audio signature to the audioMediaTypeSignatures array |
| packages/ai/src/util/detect-media-type.test.ts | Adds test cases for WebM detection from both bytes and base64 formats |


<details>
<summary>Comments suppressed due to low confidence (1)</summary>

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: logic -->
Potential null pointer exception in streaming usage calculation when usage values are null.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
In the streaming `doStream` method, when processing `isResponseCompletedChunk`, the code calculates `totalTokens` by adding `input_tokens` and `output_tokens` without null checking these individual values first:

```typescript
usage.totalTokens =
  value.response.usage.total_tokens ??
  value.response.usage.input_tokens +
    value.response.usage.output_tokens;
```

If either `input_tokens` or `output_tokens` is `null` or `undefined`, this addition will result in `NaN` because `null + number = NaN` and `undefined + number = NaN`. The code checks if the entire `usage` object exists but doesn't check if the individual token count properties are null.

Looking at the schema definition, the usage fields are defined as `z.number()` but could potentially be null in practice, and the non-streaming version properly handles this with null coalescing to 0.

---

### Recommendation
Add null coalescing to individual usage properties to ensure safe arithmetic:

```typescript
usage.totalTokens =
  value.response.usage.total_tokens ??
  (value.response.usage.input_tokens ?? 0) +
    (value.response.usage.output_tokens ?? 0);
```

This matches the pattern used in the non-streaming `doGenerate` method on lines 269-273.
</details>

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: type-safety -->
The URL configuration function only accepts `path` parameter but the language model calls it with both `path` and `modelId` parameters, causing a type mismatch.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
There's a mismatch between the URL function signature defined in `HuggingFaceConfig` and how it's implemented in the provider. 

The config interface at `packages/huggingface/src/huggingface-config.ts:5` defines:
```typescript
url: (options: { modelId: string; path: string }) => string;
```

But the provider implementation at line 75 only uses the `path` parameter:
```typescript
url: ({ path }) => `${baseURL}${path}`,
```

However, the language model calls this function with both parameters at lines 149-152 and 302-305:
```typescript
url: this.config.url({
  path: '/responses',
  modelId: this.modelId,
})
```

This will cause the `modelId` parameter to be ignored, which could lead to issues if the URL generation needs to be model-specific in the future. The function should either accept both parameters (even if `modelId` is unused) or the interface should be updated to reflect the actual usage.

The fix is to update the provider implementation to accept both parameters:
```typescript
url: ({ path, modelId }) => `${baseURL}${path}`,
```
</details>

body:
Tool call arguments are passed as raw strings but should be parsed as JSON objects for proper type handling.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/huggingface/src/responses/huggingface-responses-language-model.ts b/packages/huggingface/src/responses/huggingface-responses-language-model.ts index 541aede4c..2da7eb29a 100644 --- a/packages/huggingface/src/responses/huggingface-responses-language-model.ts +++ b/packages/huggingface/src/responses/huggingface-responses-language-model.ts @@ -222,7 +222,7 @@ export class HuggingFaceResponsesLanguageModel implements LanguageModelV2 { type: 'tool-call', toolCallId: part.id, toolName: part.name, - input: part.arguments, + input: JSON.parse(part.arguments), providerExecuted: true, }); @@ -264,7 +264,7 @@ export class HuggingFaceResponsesLanguageModel implements LanguageModelV2 { type: 'tool-call', toolCallId: part.call_id, toolName: part.name, - input: part.arguments, + input: JSON.parse(part.arguments), }); if (part.output) { @@ -420,7 +420,7 @@ export class HuggingFaceResponsesLanguageModel implements LanguageModelV2 { type: 'tool-call', toolCallId: value.item.call_id, toolName: value.item.name, - input: value.item.arguments, + input: JSON.parse(value.item.arguments), }); if (value.item.output) { ```
### Analysis In the `doGenerate` method, when processing `mcp_call` and `function_call` output items, the code directly passes `part.arguments` as the `input` field without parsing it from JSON string to object (lines 225, 267). According to the schema definitions on lines 555 and 564, the `arguments` field is defined as `z.string()`, indicating it comes from the API as a JSON string. However, the AI SDK's `LanguageModelV2Content` expects the tool call input to be a parsed object, not a string. This mismatch will cause tool calls to receive string arguments instead of properly structured objects, potentially breaking tool execution. The same issue occurs in the streaming implementation at line 423 where `value.item.arguments` is passed directly. The fix is to parse these JSON strings before passing them to the content array: ```typescript input: JSON.parse(part.arguments) ``` This ensures that tools receive properly structured argument objects as expected by the framework.

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: security -->
JSON injection vulnerability in MCP list_tools tool call input construction due to unescaped user-controlled data.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
# JSON injection vulnerability in MCP list_tools input construction

**What fails:** HuggingFaceResponsesLanguageModel constructs JSON using unsafe template literals in `mcp_list_tools` case, allowing MCP servers to inject arbitrary JSON properties through crafted `server_label` values.

**How to reproduce:**
```javascript
// MCP server returns malicious server_label:
const mcpResponse = { 
  type: 'mcp_list_tools', 
  server_label: 'test","admin":true,"bypass":"security' 
};
// Results in: {"server_label": "test","admin":true,"bypass":"security"}
// Creates valid JSON with injected properties: {server_label: "test", admin: true, bypass: "security"}
```

**Result:** MCP servers can inject arbitrary JSON properties into tool call inputs. Line 246 uses template literals without escaping: `input: \`{"server_label": "${part.server_label}"}\``

**Expected:** JSON should be properly escaped to prevent injection attacks, as documented in [OWASP JSON Injection Prevention](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) and highlighted in recent [MCP security research](https://www.cyberark.com/resources/threat-research-blog/poison-everywhere-no-output-from-your-mcp-server-is-safe)
</details>

The export for `HuggingFaceErrorData` incorrectly references `OpenAICompatibleErrorData` from `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`\, but the actual implementation uses a different error schema defined in `huggingface-error.ts`\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## Incorrect export type alias for HuggingFaceErrorData

**What fails\:** `packages/huggingface/src/index.ts` exports `OpenAICompatibleErrorData as HuggingFaceErrorData` but the actual implementation uses a different error schema with incompatible types

**How to reproduce\:**

```typescript
import { HuggingFaceErrorData } from '@ai-sdk/huggingface';
import { OpenAICompatibleErrorData } from '@ai-sdk/openai-compatible';

// This assignment fails due to type incompatibility
const openaiError: OpenAICompatibleErrorData = { error: { message: "test", code: 123 } };
const hfError: HuggingFaceErrorData = openaiError; // Type error: number not assignable to string
```

**Result\:** TypeScript error\: `Type 'string | number' is not assignable to type 'string'` because OpenAI\'s error\.code allows numbers while HuggingFace\'s requires strings

**Expected\:** Export should reference the actual `HuggingFaceErrorData` type defined in `./huggingface-error.ts` which is used by `huggingfaceFailedResponseHandler` in the implementation

**Fixed by\:** Changing export from `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` to `./huggingface-error` to match actual error handling implementation

</details>

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: type-safety -->
Type inconsistency between schema validation and TypeScript types for the `size` field allows strings that don't match the expected format.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
The Zod schema validates `size` as either `'auto'` or a string matching the regex `/^\d+x\d+$/` (line 8), which only allows numeric width x height formats like "1024x768". However, the TypeScript type definition (line 21) includes `| string` in addition to `'auto' | `${number}x${number}``, which allows any string to pass through TypeScript compilation.

This inconsistency means that while Zod will correctly reject invalid size strings at runtime, TypeScript won't catch these errors at compile time. Users could pass invalid size values like "large" or "small" and only discover the error when the schema validation runs, rather than getting immediate feedback from their IDE or TypeScript compiler.

The fix is to remove `| string` from the TypeScript type definition on line 21, making it match the schema's more restrictive validation: `size?: 'auto' | `${number}x${number}``.
</details>

body:
The tool schema defines optional parameters like `depth`, `includeDomains`, `excludeDomains`, `fromDate`, `toDate`, and `includeImage`, but the execute function ignores all of them and only uses `query`.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/content/cookbook/05-node/56-web-search-agent.mdx b/content/cookbook/05-node/56-web-search-agent.mdx index 42f9d7120..2c89e884b 100644 --- a/content/cookbook/05-node/56-web-search-agent.mdx +++ b/content/cookbook/05-node/56-web-search-agent.mdx @@ -124,16 +124,16 @@ export const linkupWebSearch = tool({ toDate: z.string().datetime().optional().describe('Search before this date'), includeImage: z.boolean().optional().describe('Include an image'), }), - execute: async ({ query }) => { + execute: async ({ query, depth = 'standard', includeDomains, excludeDomains, fromDate, toDate, includeImage }) => { return await client.search({ query: query, - depth: 'standard', // (standard / deep) "standard" returns results faster; "deep" takes longer but yields more comprehensive results. + depth: depth, outputType: 'searchResults', - // includeImage: (true / false) To receive image results alongside text results in your search responses (set by default to false) - // includeDomains: ["example1.com", "example2.com"] // To include domain(s) - // excludeDomains: ["example1.com", "example2.com"] // To exclude domain(s) - // toDate: In Date type for eg: new Date("2024-01-01") content published or updated before the specified date - // fromDate: In Date type for eg: new Date("2024-12-31") content published after the specified date + includeImages: includeImage, + includeDomains: includeDomains, + excludeDomains: excludeDomains, + toDate: toDate ? new Date(toDate) : undefined, + fromDate: fromDate ? new Date(fromDate) : undefined, }); }, }); ```
### Analysis The `linkupWebSearch` tool has a significant mismatch between its input schema and implementation. The schema defines 6 optional parameters (`depth`, `includeDomains`, `excludeDomains`, `fromDate`, `toDate`, `includeImage`) that users can pass, but the `execute` function only destructures `query` from the input and completely ignores all other parameters. This means: 1. Users following the documentation will expect to be able to pass these parameters to customize their search 2. The parameters will be silently ignored, leading to unexpected behavior 3. All searches will use hardcoded values (`depth: 'standard'`, `outputType: 'searchResults'`) regardless of user input The fix is to either: 1. Remove the unused parameters from the schema to match the simple implementation, or 2. Update the execute function to actually use the provided parameters: ```ts execute: async ({ query, depth = 'standard', includeDomains, excludeDomains, fromDate, toDate, includeImage }) => { return await client.search({ query: query, depth: depth, outputType: 'searchResults', includeImage: includeImage, includeDomains: includeDomains, excludeDomains: excludeDomains, toDate: toDate ? new Date(toDate) : undefined, fromDate: fromDate ? new Date(fromDate) : undefined, }); }, ``` This inconsistency between schema and implementation would cause the tool to not work as documented, misleading users about its capabilities.

The function incorrectly adds spacing between prompt and schema sections, causing an extra newline when both are present.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
In the `injectJsonInstruction` function, line 27 has a logic error where it adds an empty string (which becomes a newline after `join('\n')`) when a prompt is present. This is intended to create proper spacing between the prompt and schema sections, but the current logic adds the empty string in the wrong condition.

The current code:
```typescript
prompt != null && prompt.length > 0 ? '' : undefined
```

This adds an empty string when there IS a prompt, but the array structure already includes the prompt on line 26. This creates an unnecessary third element in the array that becomes an extra newline.

Looking at the test expectations, when both prompt and schema are present, the expected format is:
```
Generate a person\n\nJSON schema:\n...
```

But the current implementation would produce:
```  
Generate a person\n\n\nJSON schema:\n...
```

The issue is that the function is trying to conditionally add spacing, but the spacing logic is incorrect.

---

### Recommendation
Replace line 27 with:
```typescript
prompt != null && prompt.length > 0 && (schemaPrefix != null || schema != null || schemaSuffix != null) ? '' : undefined
```

This ensures the empty string (separator newline) is only added when there's both a prompt AND schema-related content to separate. Alternatively, simplify the logic by always including the empty string and let the filter handle it based on other conditions.
</details>

body:
The `deepToRaw` function has a potential infinite recursion bug where `deepToRaw(toRaw(input))` could loop indefinitely if `toRaw()` doesn't fully strip reactivity from the input object.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/vue/src/utils.ts b/packages/vue/src/utils.ts index fd2f98096..cb153ac06 100644 --- a/packages/vue/src/utils.ts +++ b/packages/vue/src/utils.ts @@ -7,7 +7,17 @@ export function deepToRaw(input: T): T { if (Array.isArray(input)) { return input.map(item => deepToRaw(item)) as unknown as T; } else if (isRef(input) || isReactive(input) || isProxy(input)) { - return deepToRaw(toRaw(input)); + const raw = toRaw(input); + if (raw && typeof raw === 'object') { + if (Array.isArray(raw)) { + return raw.map(item => deepToRaw(item)) as unknown as T; + } + return Object.keys(raw).reduce((acc, key) => { + (acc as any)[key] = deepToRaw((raw as any)[key]); + return acc; + }, {} as T); + } + return raw as T; } else if (input && typeof input === 'object') { return Object.keys(input).reduce((acc, key) => { (acc as any)[key] = deepToRaw((input as any)[key]); ```
### Analysis In the `deepToRaw` function, line 10 calls `deepToRaw(toRaw(input))` recursively. While `toRaw()` typically returns a non-reactive object, there are edge cases where the returned object might still contain reactive properties or be detected as reactive/proxy by Vue's detection functions. This could lead to infinite recursion and a stack overflow error. The safer approach is to extract the raw object with `toRaw()` and then directly process its properties through the object handling logic, rather than making a recursive call on the same function with the potentially still-reactive result. This is particularly concerning because this utility is used in the critical `replaceMessage` method, where a stack overflow could break the entire chat functionality. --- ### Recommendation Replace the recursive call with direct object processing: ```typescript } else if (isRef(input) || isReactive(input) || isProxy(input)) { const raw = toRaw(input); if (raw && typeof raw === 'object') { if (Array.isArray(raw)) { return raw.map(item => deepToRaw(item)) as unknown as T; } return Object.keys(raw).reduce((acc, key) => { (acc as any)[key] = deepToRaw((raw as any)[key]); return acc; }, {} as T); } return raw as T; } ``` This approach avoids the recursive call on the same input and directly processes the raw object's properties, eliminating the infinite recursion risk.

This appears to be a logic error where the schema parameter should either be omitted (if the function can handle undefined schemas) or the condition should be adjusted to match the intended behavior. The old behavior passed the schema regardless of whether it was defined, but the new behavior creates a contradiction. --- ### Recommendation Either remove the `schema: responseFormat.schema` parameter from the function call since it will always be `undefined`, or adjust the conditional logic to match the intended behavior. <!-- VADE-CATEGORY: logic -->
When `structuredOutputs` is `false` but a JSON schema is provided, the model won't receive any schema information, causing it to generate unstructured JSON instead of following the schema.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
The logic for JSON instruction injection has a bug when `structuredOutputs` is disabled but a JSON response format with schema is requested. Currently, the code only injects JSON instructions when there's no schema (`!responseFormat?.schema` on line 118), but when `structuredOutputs` is `false`, the code falls back to using `{ type: 'json_object' }` format without the schema information (line 151).

This means when:
1. `responseFormat.type === 'json'`  
2. `responseFormat.schema` exists
3. `structuredOutputs === false`

The condition on line 118 evaluates to `false` (because schema exists), so no JSON instructions are injected, and the condition on line 141 also evaluates to `false` (because `structuredOutputs` is false), so it uses `json_object` format without schema information. The model receives no guidance about the expected JSON structure, likely producing unstructured output instead of following the provided schema.

---

### Recommendation
Update the condition on line 118 to inject JSON instructions when either there's no schema OR when there's a schema but `structuredOutputs` is disabled:

```typescript
if (responseFormat?.type === 'json' && (!responseFormat?.schema || !structuredOutputs)) {
```

This ensures that JSON instructions with schema information are injected when `structuredOutputs` is disabled, providing the model with the necessary schema guidance through the fallback instruction method.
</details>

body: We need the performance client because the existing `OpenAICompatibleEmbeddingModel` is sending large batches of 2048 strings for embedding, but Baseten has a maximum batch size limit of 128 strings. The `OpenAICompatibleEmbeddingModel` approach will fail with HTTP 422 errors. The performance client acts as an intelligent "reverse splitter/fanout" that takes large batches and distributes them into smaller chunks (e.g., 32 batches of 64 strings) across multiple replicas/machines, enabling parallel processing and faster throughput. https://www.baseten.co/blog/your-client-code-matters-10x-higher-embedding-throughput-with-python-and-rust/

body:
Hey @gr2m, the package is cross compiled to all platforms with node 14+. The package has no dependecies to other node packages (rust binary bundled with NAPI) 

Its mostly a performance optimization. For embeddings, splitting up e.g. 2048 embeddings into sizes of 4, results in better horizontal load balancing (you can queue them, estimate number of replicas for your deployment better). 

Adding an additional hope (reverse proxy as alex mentioned above) leads to issues with propagating cancellation. 

Usually, this results in around ~4x thoughput for the customer. We have a customer that runs ~1M RPM on this package.

📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/content/cookbook/00-guides/01-rag-chatbot.mdx b/content/cookbook/00-guides/01-rag-chatbot.mdx index b35fa83eb..5e8229bac 100644 --- a/content/cookbook/00-guides/01-rag-chatbot.mdx +++ b/content/cookbook/00-guides/01-rag-chatbot.mdx @@ -411,6 +411,10 @@ Alternatively, for Upstash Search, update the file like this: ```tsx filename="lib/actions/resources.ts" 'use server'; +import { + NewResourceParams, + insertResourceSchema, +} from '@/lib/db/schema/resources'; import { Search } from '@upstash/search'; type ChunkContent = { @@ -426,13 +430,9 @@ const search = new Search({ const index = search.index('knowledge-base'); -export const createResource = async (input: { content: string }) => { +export const createResource = async (input: NewResourceParams) => { try { - const { content } = input; - - if (!content) { - return { error: 'Content is required' }; - } + const { content } = insertResourceSchema.parse(input); // Chunk and store directly in Upstash Search const chunks = content @@ -453,9 +453,11 @@ export const createResource = async (input: { content: string }) => { })), ); - return { success: true }; + return 'Resource successfully created and embedded.'; } catch (error) { - return { error: 'Failed to create resource' }; + return error instanceof Error && error.message.length > 0 + ? error.message + : 'Error, please try again.'; } }; ``` ```
### Analysis The Upstash Search implementation of `createResource` on line 429 defines the function parameter as `input: { content: string }`, while the PostgreSQL implementation uses `input: NewResourceParams`. This creates an API compatibility issue where code written for one implementation would break when switching to the other. The PostgreSQL version also uses `insertResourceSchema.parse(input)` for validation, which suggests that `NewResourceParams` is a more complex type that includes validation rules. By changing to a simple inline type, the Upstash version loses this validation and creates inconsistent behavior. Additionally, the return types are inconsistent: the PostgreSQL version returns string messages (`'Resource successfully created and embedded.'` or error messages), while the Upstash version returns objects (`{ success: true }` or `{ error: string }`). This would break any calling code that expects string responses. --- ### Recommendation Update the Upstash Search implementation to use the same function signature as the PostgreSQL version: ```tsx export const createResource = async (input: NewResourceParams) => { try { const { content } = insertResourceSchema.parse(input); // ... rest of Upstash implementation return 'Resource successfully created and embedded.'; } catch (error) { return error instanceof Error && error.message.length > 0 ? error.message : 'Error, please try again.'; } }; ``` This ensures API compatibility between both implementations and maintains consistent validation and return types.

On line 108, the Upstash Search index is created without the generic type parameter:

```ts
const index = search.index('knowledge-base');
```

```ts

content: hit.content.text || '',
```

To fix this issue, line 108 should be changed to:

```ts
const index = search.index<KnowledgeContent>('knowledge-base');
```

The `mediaTypeToExtension` function doesn't handle malformed media types, which could result in `undefined` file extensions when the filename is constructed.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.test.ts b/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.test.ts index 16d4e8deb..bd435ddb5 100644 --- a/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.test.ts +++ b/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.test.ts @@ -15,4 +15,11 @@ describe('mediaTypeToExtension()', () => { expect(mediaTypeToExtension('audio/flac')).toBe('flac'); expect(mediaTypeToExtension('audio/aac')).toBe('aac'); }); + + it('should handle malformed media types gracefully', () => { + expect(mediaTypeToExtension('invalid')).toBe('bin'); + expect(mediaTypeToExtension('')).toBe('bin'); + expect(mediaTypeToExtension('/')).toBe('bin'); + expect(mediaTypeToExtension('audio')).toBe('bin'); + }); }); diff --git a/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.ts b/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.ts index 42cc71ec4..9a1032f9f 100644 --- a/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.ts +++ b/packages/provider-utils/src/media-type-to-extension.ts @@ -8,7 +8,12 @@ * @see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/MIME_types/Common_types */ export function mediaTypeToExtension(mediaType: string) { - const [_type, subtype] = mediaType.split('/'); + const parts = mediaType.split('/'); + const subtype = parts[1]; + + if (!subtype) { + return 'bin'; // fallback for malformed media types + } return ( { ```
### Analysis The function uses destructuring assignment `const [_type, subtype] = mediaType.split('/')` without validating the input format. If `mediaType` doesn't contain a '/' character (e.g., "invalid" or empty string), `subtype` becomes `undefined`. The return statement `return ({...}[subtype] || subtype)` then evaluates to `undefined`, causing the filename in the FormData.append call to become `audio.undefined`. While IANA media types should be properly formatted as "type/subtype", defensive programming practices suggest handling edge cases to prevent potential runtime issues. This could manifest as: - Malformed filenames sent to the Groq API - Potential API rejection due to invalid filename format - Unclear error messages when debugging upload failures --- ### Recommendation Add input validation to handle malformed media types gracefully. Consider adding a guard clause or default fallback: ```typescript export function mediaTypeToExtension(mediaType: string) { const parts = mediaType.split('/'); const subtype = parts[1]; if (!subtype) { return 'bin'; // or throw an error for invalid format } return ( { mpeg: 'mp3', 'x-wav': 'wav', opus: 'ogg', mp4: 'm4a', 'x-m4a': 'm4a', }[subtype] || subtype ); } ``` Alternatively, add validation at the function entry or add test cases covering these edge cases.

The codemod inconsistently reports warnings - using `context.messages.push()` for member expressions but `console.warn()` for identifiers.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
In the `not-implemented.ts` codemod, there's an inconsistency in how warnings are reported between the two code paths:

1. **Member expression path (lines 90-92)**: Uses `context.messages.push()` which properly integrates with the codemod framework and reports messages through `api.report()`
2. **Identifier path (lines 117-119)**: Uses `console.warn()` which bypasses the framework's message reporting system

This inconsistency means that warnings for simple identifier matches (like `appendClientMessage`, `appendResponseMessages`) will be logged directly to console instead of being reported through the proper codemod reporting mechanism. This could cause issues with tooling that expects all codemod messages to go through the standard reporting channel.

The fix is to change line 117-119 from:
```typescript
console.warn(
  `Warning: Found usage of "${keyword}" in ${fileInfo.path}. ${message}`,
);
```

to:
```typescript
context.messages.push(
  `Warning: Found usage of "${keyword}" in ${fileInfo.path}. ${message}`,
);
```

I've since simplified the code quite a bit, see new code in the files tab. I now leave the original providerMetadata logic unchanged and treat gateway as a special case to accomplish what I want.

The issue I ran into was that gateway `providerMetadata` was coming back as:

```
gateway: {
  images: [],
}
```

The images array would always be empty (as expected), and none of the routing/cost info would come through.

I dug through the code and realized this is because the `generate-image` providerMetadata-building code would drop all non `images` fields in this line: `providerMetadata[providerName] ??= { images: [] };`. This also had the side effect of producing an images array for every provider, which doesn't apply to gateway.

To solve this, my code preserves the `metadata` (routing/cost info) and deletes the `images` field if present and empty for the gateway provider only
author: R-Taneja

body:
I think some edit like this makes sense based on the below summary and some contemplation. @gr2m may have more background or other thoughts on approach and best practices.

Sharing as it helped me -- a sonnet-4.5 summary:

The original code had a simple merging strategy for provider metadata across multiple image generation calls...

- For __every provider__ in the metadata, it would:

  1. Initialize with `{ images: [] }` if not already present
  2. Append all images from that provider's metadata to the accumulated `images` array

- This worked fine for providers like OpenAI/Vertex that return per-image metadata in the `images` array

The new code adds special handling for the gateway provider:

__For `gateway` provider:__

- __Spreads all metadata fields__ (not just `images`) - this preserves fields like `routing`, `cost`, `marketCost`, `generationId`
- __Removes empty `images` arrays__ - the gateway doesn't provide per-image metadata, so empty arrays are noise
- __Last-write-wins__ for non-image fields across multiple calls (see test "should merge non-image provider metadata fields")

__For other providers (OpenAI, Vertex, etc.):__

- __Keeps the original behavior__ - accumulates `images` arrays across calls
- This preserves per-image metadata like `revisedPrompt` that these providers return

- __Gateway-specific metadata structure__: The AI Gateway returns operational metadata (`routing`, `cost`, `generationId`) that shouldn't be treated like per-image metadata. The old code would try to push these into an `images` array, which doesn't make sense.

- __Cleaner API surface__: Removing empty `images: []` from gateway metadata prevents confusion - if there's no per-image data, don't include the field.

- __Multi-call scenarios__: When `n > maxImagesPerCall`, multiple API calls are made. The new logic correctly:

  - Accumulates per-image metadata for providers that support it
  - Merges operational metadata for the gateway (with last-write-wins for conflicts)

- __Backward compatibility__: Non-gateway providers continue to work exactly as before.

### Analysis
# Cohere Thinking Type Default Value Inconsistency

## Issue Summary

There is a significant inconsistency between the documentation and implementation regarding the default value of the `type` field in the `thinking` parameter for Cohere chat options.

## Documentation vs Implementation

### Documented Behavior
In `packages/cohere/src/cohere-chat-options.ts` at line 23, the JSDoc documentation states:

> `type` can be set to `'enabled'` or `'disabled'` (defaults to `'disabled'`)

### Actual Implementation
In `packages/cohere/src/cohere-chat-language-model.ts` at line 128, the implementation shows:

```typescript
type: cohereOptions.thinking.type ?? 'enabled'
```

This means when thinking options are provided but the `type` field is not explicitly specified, the implementation defaults to `'enabled'`, not `'disabled'` as documented.

## Impact

This inconsistency can lead to unexpected behavior for users who:

1. **Rely on documentation**: Users expecting the default to be `'disabled'` may be surprised when thinking is actually enabled
2. **Assume conservative defaults**: Users may expect reasoning to be opt-in (disabled by default) for performance or cost considerations
3. **Integration issues**: Applications built with the assumption that thinking defaults to disabled may experience unexpected API behavior

## Code Context

The issue manifests in this logic:

```typescript
// In cohere-chat-language-model.ts line 126-132
...(cohereOptions.thinking && {
  thinking: {
    type: cohereOptions.thinking.type ?? 'enabled', // ← This defaults to 'enabled'
    token_budget: cohereOptions.thinking.tokenBudget,
  },
})
```

When a user provides a `thinking` object like `{ tokenBudget: 1000 }` without specifying `type`, the implementation will set `type: 'enabled'`, contrary to the documented default of `'disabled'`.

## Resolution Needed

The documentation and implementation should be aligned. Given that providing thinking options likely indicates intent to use the reasoning feature, the implementation's behavior of defaulting to `'enabled'` seems reasonable. Therefore, the documentation should be updated to reflect this actual behavior.
</details>

### Analysis
# Cohere Reasoning Example Incorrect Property Access

## Bug Description

The Cohere reasoning streaming example in `examples/ai-core/src/stream-text/cohere-reasoning.ts` incorrectly accesses the `text` property on `reasoning-delta` events, but these events actually provide reasoning content through a `delta` property.

## Current Behavior

At line 18 of the example file:

```typescript
if (part.type === 'reasoning-delta') {
  process.stdout.write('\x1b[34m' + part.text + '\x1b[0m');
}
```

This code attempts to access `part.text`, but `reasoning-delta` events from the Cohere provider don't have a `text` property.

## Expected Behavior

Based on the Cohere provider implementation in `packages/cohere/src/cohere-chat-language-model.ts` (line ~308), reasoning-delta events are created with this structure:

```typescript
controller.enqueue({
  type: 'reasoning-delta',
  id: String(value.index),
  delta: value.delta.message.content.thinking, // Content is in 'delta' property
});
```

## Evidence from Tests

The test expectations in `packages/cohere/src/cohere-chat-language-model.test.ts` confirm the correct event structure:

```typescript
{
  "delta": "So",           // ✅ Content in 'delta' property
  "id": "0", 
  "type": "reasoning-delta",
},
```

## Impact

This bug causes the reasoning text to display as `undefined` instead of showing the actual reasoning content, making the example completely non-functional for its intended purpose of demonstrating Cohere's reasoning capabilities.

## Fix Required

The example should access `part.delta` instead of `part.text`:

```typescript
if (part.type === 'reasoning-delta') {
  process.stdout.write('\x1b[34m' + part.delta + '\x1b[0m');
}
```
</details>

### Analysis
# Schema Validation Bug: tokenBudget Parameter Missing Constraints

## Issue Description

The `tokenBudget` parameter in the `cohereChatModelOptions` schema lacks proper validation constraints, allowing invalid values that contradict the documented requirements.

## Technical Details

**Location**: `packages/cohere/src/cohere-chat-options.ts`, line 31

**Current Schema**:
```typescript
tokenBudget: z.number().optional(),
```

**Expected Schema**:
```typescript
tokenBudget: z.number().int().positive().optional(),
```

## Problem Manifestation

The current schema validation accepts all of the following invalid inputs:

- **Negative numbers**: `{ thinking: { tokenBudget: -5 } }` ✅ (should fail)
- **Zero**: `{ thinking: { tokenBudget: 0 } }` ✅ (should fail)  
- **Decimal numbers**: `{ thinking: { tokenBudget: 5.5 } }` ✅ (should fail)

While the documentation comment clearly states that `tokenBudget` "must be set to a positive integer", the schema validation doesn't enforce this requirement.

## Why This Is Problematic

1. **API Contract Violation**: Values that pass client-side validation may be rejected by the Cohere API, leading to runtime errors
2. **Logical Inconsistency**: Token counts cannot be negative, zero (would disable thinking), or fractional
3. **Developer Confusion**: The mismatch between documentation and validation creates confusion about valid inputs
4. **Poor User Experience**: Invalid configurations aren't caught until API calls are made

## Impact

- Users can configure invalid token budgets that will fail at runtime
- Debugging becomes harder when validation passes locally but API calls fail
- The SDK doesn't provide proper input validation as expected

## Supporting Evidence

Based on [Cohere's reasoning documentation](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/reasoning), token budgets are used to limit thinking tokens, with recommendations for values between 1K-31K tokens. The API logically requires positive integers for token counting.

Testing confirms the current schema permits all invalid cases while the proposed fix correctly rejects them while preserving valid positive integer values.
</details>

The `onChunk` callback is not wrapped in try/catch, so if it throws an error, it will crash the stream processing instead of gracefully handling the error through the `onError` callback.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/ai/src/generate-object/stream-object.ts b/packages/ai/src/generate-object/stream-object.ts index a559a78b8..ca11038fc 100644 --- a/packages/ai/src/generate-object/stream-object.ts +++ b/packages/ai/src/generate-object/stream-object.ts @@ -486,7 +486,11 @@ class DefaultStreamObjectResult controller.enqueue(chunk); if (chunk.type === 'object' || chunk.type === 'text-delta') { - await onChunk?.({ chunk }); + try { + await onChunk?.({ chunk }); + } catch (error) { + await onError({ error }); + } } if (chunk.type === 'error') { diff --git a/packages/ai/src/generate-text/stream-text.ts b/packages/ai/src/generate-text/stream-text.ts index 968844d37..7adf30a9d 100644 --- a/packages/ai/src/generate-text/stream-text.ts +++ b/packages/ai/src/generate-text/stream-text.ts @@ -680,7 +680,11 @@ class DefaultStreamTextResult part.type === 'tool-input-delta' || part.type === 'raw' ) { - await onChunk?.({ chunk: part }); + try { + await onChunk?.({ chunk: part }); + } catch (error) { + await onError({ error }); + } } if (part.type === 'error') { ```
### Analysis In the `transform` function of the `eventProcessor` TransformStream, the `onChunk` callback is awaited without any error handling: ```typescript if (chunk.type === 'object' || chunk.type === 'text-delta') { await onChunk?.({ chunk }); } ``` If the user-provided `onChunk` callback throws an error (either synchronously or asynchronously), it will cause the entire stream to error and terminate abruptly. This is inconsistent with the error handling pattern used elsewhere in the codebase where errors are caught and processed through the `onError` callback. The fix should wrap the `onChunk` call in a try/catch block and route any errors to the `onError` callback, similar to how other errors are handled in the stream processing pipeline. This ensures graceful error handling and prevents user callback errors from crashing the stream.

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: type-safety -->
The codemod will crash when encountering object spread syntax (e.g., `{...obj, maxSteps: 5}`) because it tries to access `.key` on SpreadElement nodes which don't have that property.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
The removal of `j.Property.check(prop) &&` from the `findIndex` predicate (lines 31-32) and `!j.Property.check(maxStepsProp) ||` from the validation check (lines 37-38) introduces a critical bug. 

In JavaScript AST, `ObjectExpression.properties` can contain both `Property` nodes and `SpreadElement` nodes (from object spread syntax like `{...obj, maxSteps: 5}`). SpreadElement nodes don't have a `key` property, so accessing `prop.key.name` or `prop.key.value` on a SpreadElement will cause a runtime error.

The original code correctly filtered to only Property nodes before accessing their `.key` property. Without this check, the codemod will crash with "Cannot read property 'name' of undefined" when processing any object that contains spread elements.

Other codemods in the same codebase (like `move-image-model-maxImagesPerCall.ts` and `rename-max-tokens-to-max-output-tokens.ts`) explicitly check for `prop.type === 'Property' || prop.type === 'ObjectProperty'` before accessing properties, following the correct pattern.

The fix is to restore the property type checks: `j.Property.check(prop) &&` in the findIndex predicate and `!j.Property.check(maxStepsProp) ||` in the validation.
</details>

body:
The codemod only checks for `j.ObjectProperty` but should check for both `j.Property` and `j.ObjectProperty` to ensure compatibility across different AST representations.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/codemod/src/codemods/v5/move-maxsteps-to-stopwhen.ts b/packages/codemod/src/codemods/v5/move-maxsteps-to-stopwhen.ts index 5621cbd35..81d9c4e9e 100644 --- a/packages/codemod/src/codemods/v5/move-maxsteps-to-stopwhen.ts +++ b/packages/codemod/src/codemods/v5/move-maxsteps-to-stopwhen.ts @@ -28,7 +28,7 @@ export default createTransformer((fileInfo, api, options, context) => { return false; const maxStepsPropIdx = objExpr.properties.findIndex( (prop: any) => - j.ObjectProperty.check(prop) && + (j.Property.check(prop) || j.ObjectProperty.check(prop)) && ((j.Identifier.check(prop.key) && prop.key.name === 'maxSteps') || (j.StringLiteral.check(prop.key) && prop.key.value === 'maxSteps')), ); @@ -36,7 +36,7 @@ export default createTransformer((fileInfo, api, options, context) => { const maxStepsProp = objExpr.properties[maxStepsPropIdx]; if ( - !j.ObjectProperty.check(maxStepsProp) || + (!j.Property.check(maxStepsProp) && !j.ObjectProperty.check(maxStepsProp)) || (!j.Literal.check(maxStepsProp.value) && !j.Identifier.check(maxStepsProp.value) && !j.BinaryExpression.check(maxStepsProp.value)) ```
### Analysis The change from `j.Property.check(prop)` to `j.ObjectProperty.check(prop)` at lines 31 and 39 fixes compatibility with some file types, but it's too restrictive. Looking at other codemods in the codebase (like `rename-mime-type-to-media-type.ts` and `replace-content-with-parts.ts`), the standard pattern is to check for both property types: `j.Property.check(prop) || j.ObjectProperty.check(prop)`. Different TypeScript/JavaScript parsers and contexts can represent object properties as either `Property` or `ObjectProperty` nodes in the AST. By only checking for `ObjectProperty`, the codemod may miss legitimate `maxSteps` properties that are represented as `Property` nodes, causing the transformation to be skipped in some files. The fix should be to check for both types: `(j.Property.check(prop) || j.ObjectProperty.check(prop)) &&` at line 31 and `(!j.Property.check(maxStepsProp) && !j.ObjectProperty.check(maxStepsProp)) ||` at line 39.

### Analysis The code directly accesses `part.output.value as string` on line 160 without first validating that `part.output` has the expected structure. Based on the test cases, the expected structure is `{ type: 'text', value: string }`, but this is not guaranteed. If `part.output` is a different type (e.g., a string directly, null, or an object without a `value` property), this will cause a runtime error when trying to access the `value` property on `undefined` or a non-object. The code should either: 1. Add type guards to check the structure: `if (part.output && typeof part.output === 'object' && 'value' in part.output)` 2. Use optional chaining: `part.output?.value` 3. Implement proper type validation for the expected output structure This is particularly important since this code handles external API responses where the structure may vary or evolve.

The default case in `formatWarning()` calls `JSON.stringify()` without error handling, which could throw an exception if the warning object contains circular references or non-serializable values.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/packages/ai/src/logger/log-warnings.ts b/packages/ai/src/logger/log-warnings.ts index a283cb143..80e14d77c 100644 --- a/packages/ai/src/logger/log-warnings.ts +++ b/packages/ai/src/logger/log-warnings.ts @@ -44,7 +44,13 @@ function formatWarning(warning: Warning): string { default: { // Fallback for any unknown warning types - return `${prefix} ${JSON.stringify(warning, null, 2)}`; + try { + return `${prefix} ${JSON.stringify(warning, null, 2)}`; + } catch { + // JSON.stringify might fail if the warning object contains circular references + // or other non-serializable values, in which case we provide a safe fallback + return `${prefix} [Unserializable warning object]`; + } } } } ```
### Analysis In the `formatWarning()` function, the default case uses `JSON.stringify(warning, null, 2)` to serialize unknown warning types. This can throw an exception if the warning object contains circular references, functions, symbols, or other non-serializable values. Since this is a logging function that should be resilient and not crash the application, it should handle potential `JSON.stringify()` errors gracefully. The fix would be to wrap the `JSON.stringify()` call in a try-catch block and fall back to a safe string representation if serialization fails, such as: ```typescript default: { try { return `${prefix} ${JSON.stringify(warning, null, 2)}`; } catch { return `${prefix} [Unserializable warning object]`; } } ```
